question.prompt:
Isosceles \(\triangle ABC\) has a right angle at \(C.\) Point \(P\) is inside \(\triangle ABC,\) such that \(PA = 11,\) \(PB = 7,\) and \(PC = 6.\) Legs \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{BC}\) have length \(s = \sqrt{a + b\sqrt{2}},\) where \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers. What is \(a + b?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2006_AMC_12B_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The perpendicular equal legs make convenient coordinate axes. Subtracting the squared distance equations will cancel the repeated terms involving \(P\).

[Figure 1](figures/2006_AMC_12B_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

Place \(C=(0,0)\), \(A=(s,0)\), and \(B=(0,s)\), where \(s>0\). Write \(P=(x,y)\). Since \(P\) is inside the triangle,
\[
x>0,\qquad y>0,\qquad x+y<s.
\]
The three distances give
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2+y^2&=36,\\
(s-x)^2+y^2&=121,\\
x^2+(s-y)^2&=49.
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtracting the first equation from each of the other two yields
\[
2sx=s^2-85,\qquad 2sy=s^2-13.
\]
Let \(t=s^2>0\). Because \(s>0\) and \(x>0\), the first relation also shows that \(t>85\). Dividing by the nonzero number \(2s\) and substituting into \(x^2+y^2=36\) gives
\[
(t-85)^2+(t-13)^2=144t.
\]
Expanding and completing the square,
\[
\begin{aligned}
t^2-170t+3697&=0,\\
(t-85)^2&=3528=2\cdot42^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(t=85\pm42\sqrt2\). The condition \(t>85\) excludes the minus sign, leaving \(t=85+42\sqrt2\).

To check interiority for this value, recover
\[
x=\frac{t-85}{2\sqrt t}>0,
\qquad y=\frac{t-13}{2\sqrt t}>0.
\]
Also,
\[
x+y=\frac{t-49}{\sqrt t}<\sqrt t=s.
\]
The equation for \(t\) ensures \(x^2+y^2=36\), and the two subtraction relations then give the other two original squared distances. Hence this value satisfies all the conditions.

We have \(s=\sqrt{85+42\sqrt2}\). Since \(\sqrt2\) is irrational, its integer coefficients are uniquely determined: \(a=85\) and \(b=42\). Therefore \(a+b=\boxed{127}\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
solutions.title: Subtract coordinate distance equations

solutions.explanation:
A quarter-turn can turn the distance \(PC=6\) into a segment of length \(6\sqrt2\). This is useful because
\[
7^2+(6\sqrt2)^2=11^2.
\]
Rotate the triangle and \(P\) through \(90^\circ\) about \(C\), in the direction carrying \(A\) to \(B\). Let \(Q\) be the image of \(P\). Rotation preserves lengths, so
\[
BQ=AP=11,\qquad CQ=CP=6,
\]
and \(\angle PCQ=90^\circ\). Thus triangle \(CPQ\) is isosceles and right, giving
\[
PQ=6\sqrt2,\qquad \angle CPQ=45^\circ.
\]
We also need the positions of these rays. If \(T\) is the image of \(B\), then \(A,C,T\) are collinear with \(C\) between \(A\) and \(T\). The original triangle \(ABC\) and its rotated copy \(BCT\) form the larger triangle \(ABT\), sharing side \(BC\). Since \(P\) and \(Q\) lie inside the two respective halves, segment \(PQ\) crosses the interior of \(BC\). Therefore ray \(PQ\) lies inside \(\angle CPB\).

Now
\[
BQ^2=11^2=7^2+(6\sqrt2)^2=BP^2+PQ^2.
\]
The converse of the Pythagorean theorem gives \(\angle BPQ=90^\circ\). Consequently,
\[
\angle CPB=45^\circ+90^\circ=135^\circ.
\]
Because this angle is obtuse, the perpendicular from \(C\) to line \(BP\) meets its extension beyond \(P\), at a point \(H\). Triangle \(CPH\) has angles \(45^\circ,45^\circ,90^\circ\), so its legs are equal. Since its hypotenuse is \(CP=6\), the Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
PH=CH=3\sqrt2.
\]
With \(B,P,H\) in that order, \(BH=7+3\sqrt2\). Applying the Pythagorean theorem to triangle \(BHC\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
s^2=BC^2
&=(7+3\sqrt2)^2+(3\sqrt2)^2\\
&=85+42\sqrt2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The irrationality of \(\sqrt2\) makes the integer coefficients unique, so \(a=85\), \(b=42\), and \(a+b=\boxed{127}\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
solutions.title: Rotate to construct a right triangle
